description: Test your knowledge of Introduction to hematology.

cards.text: What are the two defining properties of a haematopoietic stem cell (HSC)?
cards.answer: Self-renewal (ability to divide and produce daughter HSCs) and multipotency (ability to commit to any blood cell lineage).

tip.tip: Remember: HSCs are rare (0.01% of marrow cells) but powerful — they can both copy themselves AND become anything.

cards.text: Name the two major progenitor families that arise from the HSC and the cell types each produces.
cards.answer: CMP (common myeloid progenitor) produces RBCs, platelets, and myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils). CLP (common lymphoid progenitor) produces T cells, B cells, and NK cells.

tip.tip: CMP = everything *except* lymphocytes. CLP = lymphocytes only.

cards.text: Which hormone drives erythropoiesis and where is it produced? What stimulus increases its release?
cards.answer: Erythropoietin (EPO), produced by peritubular cells of the kidney. Release increases in hypoxia (low blood oxygen).

tip.tip: Kidney → EPO → RBCs. Hypoxia is the signal that says 'make more blood cells.'

cards.text: List the erythroid maturation sequence from earliest to most mature stage visible on a normal peripheral blood film.
cards.answer: Proerythroblast → basophilic erythroblast → polychromatic erythroblast → orthochromatic erythroblast → reticulocyte → mature erythrocyte. Only reticulocytes and mature RBCs are normally visible on PBF.

tip.tip: Normal PBF shows only the last two stages. Finding nucleated RBCs (NRBCs) on PBF is always abnormal — it signals severe stress or bone marrow disease.

cards.text: When does haemoglobin synthesis begin during erythroid maturation, and how is this visible on a blood film?
cards.answer: Haemoglobin synthesis begins at the polychromatic erythroblast stage. Cytoplasm shifts from deep blue (RNA-rich) to blue-pink (haemoglobin accumulating), then to pink (mature RBC).

tip.tip: Blue → pink colour shift = Hb being built. You can 'see' protein synthesis happening under the microscope.

cards.text: What is the significance of an elevated reticulocyte count in anaemia?
cards.answer: An elevated reticulocyte count indicates the bone marrow is responding appropriately to anaemia by increasing RBC production. A low reticulocyte count in anaemia suggests bone marrow failure (aplasia, EPO deficiency).

tip.tip: Reticulocytes = marrow's effort meter. High count = marrow is working hard. Low count in anaemia = marrow is giving up.

cards.text: How long does the entire process from EPO stimulus to mature RBC release take?
cards.answer: Approximately 7 days from EPO stimulus to mature RBC ready for release into the circulation.

tip.tip: 7 days to build a red blood cell. In health, 2 million RBCs are produced per second to maintain steady state.

cards.text: Name four key growth factors in haematopoiesis and identify which lineage each primarily drives.
cards.answer: EPO (erythropoiesis), TPO (megakaryopoiesis/platelet production), G-CSF (neutrophil production), SCF (HSC survival and proliferation).

tip.tip: Each lineage has its own growth factor 'fuel pump.' EPO and TPO are produced outside the marrow (kidney, liver); G-CSF and SCF are marrow-based.
